title: Error-Transparent Code Switching Between Permutation-Invariant Codes with Transversal Clifford and Icosahedral Gates
abstract: Code switching moves an encoded qubit between two codes whose transversal gates together are universal, but the switching operation itself is usually not transversal and can spread a single fault into an uncorrectable error. We study switching between two permutation-invariant codes on the same qubits, one with transversal Clifford gates and one with transversal gates from the non-Clifford binary icosahedral group. Both are compatible with transversal $X$, $Z$, and $F = HS^\dagger$, and the encoders with this property form a small linear space. We show that its codes of distance at least three are cut out by at most two quadratic equations, and that all of them have the same error geometry in the sense that their single-qubit error states have the same inner products. It follows that a switching unitary commuting with qubit permutations and with the shared transversal gates at every instant, and tolerating one single-qubit fault at an unknown time, exists if and only if the two codes are joined by a continuous path of distance-three codes. Such a switch can be made error transparent, so that a fault at any moment reaches the target code as the same single-qubit error. For real encoders, the distance-three codes are the solutions of a single quadratic equation, and on thirteen qubits, they form an explicit circle through two Clifford codes and an icosahedral code. We construct the switching unitary along this circle as a collective operator, leaving its synthesis into physical control open, and verify that its recovery infidelity per fault is at machine precision, whereas two natural alternatives leave average infidelities of $0.13$ and $0.85$. A survey over odd qubit numbers up to $29$ lists where such switches exist.
summary: This theoretical work establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for performing error-transparent switching between two distinct permutation-invariant quantum error-correcting codes. By linking the switch's existence to the continuous path connecting the codes through distance-three structures, the authors construct a highly accurate, fault-tolerant switching unitary. This advances the practical feasibility of modular quantum computation by ensuring robustness during code transitions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving error-transparent code switching between two different permutation-invariant quantum error-correcting codes.
main_result: An error-transparent switch exists if and only if the two codes are connected by a continuous path of distance-three codes, and the constructed unitary achieves machine-precision recovery fidelity.
method: The analysis uses algebraic constraints derived from the requirement of distance-three codes and constructs the switching unitary as a collective operator along a continuous path.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum error-correcting codes on $n$ qubits, specifically permutation-invariant (PI) codes utilizing transversal Clifford and Icosahedral gates. The switching mechanism is analyzed by examining the constancy of the error geometry along the path connecting the two codes.
key_observables: Recovery infidelity per fault, error geometry (inner products between error states), and the fidelity of the recovered channel.
important_parameters: The distance of the codes (specifically distance $\ge 3$), the fault probability ($p$), and the number of qubits ($n$, up to 29).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the switch acts on a single block without ancilla codes, and the error model is restricted to single-qubit faults.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but mention explicit constructions for 13 qubits forming a circle through Clifford and Icosahedral codes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem (error-transparent switching) to establishing necessary conditions (distance-three codes, constant error geometry), deriving the existence criterion (continuous path), and finally constructing and verifying the unitary operator.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework for ensuring fault-tolerant operations across different quantum codes is highly relevant to building large-scale quantum processors.
